title: JSON Formatter
dek: Paste messy JSON, get it neat — with a precise error message and line number when it's broken.
meta: Format, validate and minify JSON in your browser. Clear error messages with line numbers. Free, private, nothing pasted is uploaded.

steps.p: Or a piece of it — the tool tells you where the syntax breaks, line included.
Two spaces, four spaces or tabs for readability; one line for feeding to something else.
Copy button for the clipboard, or take it as a .json file.

faq.a: Trailing commas, single quotes, unquoted keys, comments — the things that make JSON look like JavaScript but aren't. The error message points at the line and character.
Very large — megabytes of JSON format in well under a second since it's a genuine parser, not a regex trick.

meta: Convert CSV to JSON in your browser, with header handling and quote-safe parsing. Copy or download the result. Free, no uploads.

steps.b: Drop a CSV or paste it
steps.p: Quoted fields, commas inside quotes, whichever line ending — handled properly.
First row as headers (the usual), or array-of-arrays for raw data.
Pretty-printed by default, one line if you switch it.

faq.a: Numbers that look like numbers become numbers; everything else stays a string. Leading zeros are kept as strings, because they mean something.
Tens of MB are fine. Beyond that your laptop starts doing the hard work, not the tool — but it will get there.

meta: Convert JSON arrays to CSV files in your browser. Columns are unioned across all objects so nothing is lost. Free and private.

steps.p: An array of objects, or an object with arrays inside.
The table preview shows exactly what the CSV will contain.
Ready for Excel, Sheets or a database import.

faq.q: What if objects have different keys?
faq.a: The CSV gets the union of all keys, so no column disappears just because the first row lacked it.
Everything is properly quoted per CSV rules — the file won't shred itself in Excel.

steps.b: Drop a spreadsheet or tabular file
steps.p: XLSX, XLS, ODS in — or CSV/JSON to build a workbook.
Multi-sheet workbooks let you convert one sheet at a time, or all of them at once.
CSV or JSON for outgoing data; a proper .xlsx for anything headed to Excel.

faq.a: Cached values are used — what you last saw in Excel is what converts. The formulas themselves live on in the original file.
The classic Excel-dates-in-CSV problem. Dates export as readable ISO values; if a column looks wrong, check the sheet's own formatting first.

The preview shows how columns and numbers were read.
Opens cleanly in Excel, Sheets, LibreOffice — you know the drill.

faq.q: Do the column widths get set?
faq.a: Auto widths are applied so you don't open a workbook of ##### instantly. Fine-tuning remains a human pleasure.
The separator is detected automatically (comma, semicolon or tab), with a manual override if the detection guesses wrong.

title: Markdown to HTML

meta: Convert Markdown to clean HTML in your browser — fragments for embedding or complete pages. GitHub-flavoured, free, no uploads.

steps.p: Tables, code blocks, task lists — GitHub-flavoured syntax is the standard here.
Rendered output updates live, next to the raw HTML.
Fragment for pasting into an existing page, or a full standalone document.

faq.q: Is the HTML safe to publish?
faq.a: Your own Markdown is. Raw HTML inside it passes through — that's standard behaviour — so treat Markdown from strangers like any other user input.
GitHub-flavoured: tables, strikethrough, auto-links, task lists. The additions most people assume are base Markdown anyway.

title: HTML to Markdown

meta: Convert HTML back into clean Markdown — headings, links, lists, emphasis and tables. Browser-based, free, private.

steps.p: Copy from a page's source, a CMS export, an email template — anything.
ATX headings (# vs underline), bullet character, code fence style. Defaults suit most people.
Ready for READMEs, docs, static site generators, notes apps.

faq.q: What about tables and code blocks?
faq.a: Both convert properly, tables included — which is where most converters give up.
No — Markdown has no place for them. The content structure survives; the decoration doesn't.

title: Diff Checker
dek: Paste two versions, see exactly what changed — line by line, or word by word for fine print.
meta: Find the difference between two texts or code files side by side, with line and word granularity. Free, private, in-browser diff.

steps.p: Left is the old, right is the new. Order of operations matters only for reading comfort.
Line view for code and lists; word view for contracts and prose, where a comma can matter.
Removed material in red, added in green, unchanged context left plain.

faq.q: Can it ignore whitespace and case?
faq.a: Yes — toggles for both. Turn them on before you accuse anyone of an edit they never made.

faq.q: Is this the same diff Git uses?
faq.a: The same algorithm family. Output is a comfortable reading view rather than a patch file you could apply.

title: Regex Tester
dek: Write a pattern, drop in sample text, watch matches highlight live — with groups, flags and a replace preview.
meta: Test JavaScript regular expressions against sample text with live highlighting, capture groups and replace preview. Free and private.

steps.p: JavaScript flavour — the same engine as your browser, so what you test here is what runs there.
Matches highlight as you type. Capture groups are listed with their content.
Use $1, $2 for group references and see the result before you commit it anywhere.

faq.a: JavaScript (ECMAScript). Python, PCRE or .NET differences — lookbehind edge cases, possessive quantifiers — won't all translate, so test in the target language too.
A browser tab can still be hung by a vicious pattern; that risk is part of regex itself, not this page. Real text behaves.

title: Case Converter

meta: Convert text between upper, lower, title, sentence, camel, snake, kebab and constant case instantly. Free, browser-based, private.

steps.p: A heading, a variable name, a shouty email — all valid inputs.
The full menu: Upper, lower, Title, Sentence, camelCase, PascalCase, snake_case, kebab-case, CONSTANT_CASE.
Same words, new wardrobe.

faq.q: Will Title Case mangle small words?
faq.a: It keeps 'and', 'of', 'the' lowercase in the middle of titles — which is the actual rule, respected.

faq.q: Does it work on text with line breaks?
faq.a: Yes, each line converts independently, so lists of identifiers survive intact.

meta: Count words, characters, sentences and paragraphs with live stats and reading time. Free, private, works offline in your browser.

Words, characters (with and without spaces), sentences, paragraphs, and reading time at 220 words per minute.
Set a target — 280 for a tweet, 160 for a meta description — and see the remainder counted down.

faq.a: 220 words per minute — the widely used average for adults reading on screens. Speech runs slower; writing runs slower still.
No. It exists in the page while you're on it and nowhere else the moment you leave.

title: Clean Up Text
dek: The tidy-up pass: remove duplicate lines, sort, trim whitespace, kill empty lines, fix curly quotes.
meta: Clean text in one pass: remove duplicate lines, sort lines, trim whitespace, remove empty lines and normalise quotes. Free and private.

steps.p: Exports, scraped lists, spreadsheet columns pasted as walls.
They stack — remove duplicates, sort alphabetically or numerically, trim each line, drop empties, straighten smart quotes.
Line count before and after, so you can see the damage undone.

faq.a: Numbers sort as numbers, so 'file2' comes before 'file10' — unlike the dictionary order that infuriates everyone.
Your call, via a toggle. 'Apple' and 'apple' can count as one line or two.

title: Base64 Encode / Decode
dek: Text to Base64 and back, with proper UTF-8 handling so emoji don't come out as confetti.
meta: Encode text to Base64 or decode Base64 back to text with full UTF-8 support. Free, instant, private — nothing leaves your browser.

steps.p: Encode for text to Base64; decode for the reverse. The tool auto-detects the sensible one.
Unicode, emoji, accented names — all handled correctly.
Also available in URL-safe Base64 if you're feeding it into a query string.

faq.q: Why is Base64 longer than the original?
faq.a: It needs about 33% more characters — that's the cost of representing any bytes with 64 safe symbols. It's encoding, not compression.
Emphatically no. It hides nothing from anyone who cares to look. Passwords and secrets belong in a password manager, not in Base64.

title: URL Encode / Decode

meta: Encode and decode URLs and query strings, including full-string and component modes. Browser-based, free, nothing uploaded.

steps.p: A full link, a query value, or a path segment.
Component mode for values (spaces become %20); full-URL mode keeps :/?&= structure intact.
Decoding works on anything percent-encoded you feed it.

faq.a: Both, via the mode switch. The first for values you're assembling into a URL, the second for an entire URL you're passing along.
Both appear in the wild; %20 is the standard form. When decoding, both are understood.

Escape turns angle brackets and ampersands into entities; unescape reverses it, named entities included.
Paste safe now.

faq.a: The five that matter in HTML: & < > " '. Everything else is left readable for humans.
Both — & and & decode equally happily.

title: Hash Generator
dek: Checksums for text or files — every SHA seen in the wild — to verify a download or fingerprint a string.
meta: Compute SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 hashes for text or files, in your browser. Verify downloads without uploading them.

steps.p: Paste a string, or drop a file to hash its full contents.
All four SHA variants are produced at once. SHA-256 is the one you want 99% of the time.
Paste the 'official' hash next to it and compare visually — or hex by hex.

faq.a: Browsers no longer expose it for good reason — it's broken for security use. If you need MD5 to match an old checksum, say so via the contact page.

faq.q: Is a hash the same as encryption?
faq.a: No — hashing is one-way by design. You can't get the file back from its hash; you can only check that another copy matches.

title: UUID Generator
dek: Version 4 UUIDs from a proper cryptographic source — one, or five hundred for that seed script.
meta: Generate random v4 UUIDs — single, bulk up to 500, with formatting options. Cryptographically secure, browser-based, free.

steps.p: One for the clipboard, hundreds for filling a database column.
Standard, uppercase, or braces-wrapped. Hyphens on or off.
One per line, ready to paste into SQL, code or a config.

faq.a: From the browser's cryptographic generator — the same source used for encryption keys. Not the 'random' of toy languages.
You'd need to generate a billion UUIDs a second for decades to have a realistic chance. Sleep easy.

title: Password Generator
dek: Long, random, actually strong — generated on your device, never transmitted, never stored.
meta: Create strong random passwords with length, symbol and ambiguity controls — generated locally in your browser. Nothing is sent anywhere.

steps.p: 16 characters is the modern floor; 20+ where the site allows it.
Uppercase, numbers, symbols — and a toggle to skip lookalikes (l/1/I, O/0) when you'll be typing it by hand.
Into a password manager, ideally. The clipboard is a hallway, not a home.

faq.a: Yes — from the browser's crypto generator, with rejection sampling so every character is equally likely. Slightly more code than the lazy version, meaningfully more entropy.

faq.q: Should I use a phrase instead?
faq.a: Long passphrases beat short passwords on strength and memorability both. Pick four diceware words, or take a 20-character random and let the manager remember it.

Classic Latin, or English words when the client reads the mockup a little too closely.
Into Figma, a CMS, an email template — wherever the real copy will eventually live.

faq.a: Because readers stop reading layouts when they see real words. Filler keeps eyes on the design, which is the whole point of a mockup.

faq.q: Does it start with 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet'?
faq.a: If you want the authentic opening, flip the toggle. Otherwise it starts anywhere in the corpus, which looks less copy-pasted.

title: Timestamp Converter
dek: Seconds or milliseconds in, human date out — and the reverse — plus the current time for reference.
meta: Convert Unix timestamps to dates and back, in seconds or milliseconds, with your local timezone and UTC shown. Free and private.

steps.p: 10 digits is seconds, 13 is milliseconds. The tool detects which and says so.
ISO strings and common date formats convert in the other direction.
Local time, UTC, ISO 8601 — all shown at once, so you can grab the format your system wants.

faq.q: Why does my timestamp look two decades off?
faq.a: The seconds-versus-milliseconds mix-up — the single most common bug in timestamp history. The tool labels which one it read, so you'll see the mistake immediately.
The date when 32-bit systems run out of seconds. Watch it happen here, live, if you paste 2147483647.
